interview.answer: HSCAN iterates a hash incrementally instead of returning the entire collection in one call. Start with cursor 0 and pass each returned cursor into the next call until the cursor returns to 0.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid blocking work on a large hash? Use repeated HSCAN calls and process each batch as it arrives, rather than using a single bulk retrieval operation.

interview.question: What do MATCH and COUNT do?
interview.answer: MATCH accepts a glob-style pattern and limits returned fields to matching names. COUNT supplies a suggested number of fields for an iteration, with a default of 10.
interview.followUp: Can MATCH guarantee that every call returns matching fields? No; filtering can produce an empty batch even while the cursor has not returned to 0.

interview.question: What does NOVALUES change?
interview.answer: Without NOVALUES, the response contains a cursor and scanned field/value pairs. With NOVALUES, Redis returns only field names; the option was introduced in Redis 7.4.
interview.followUp: When is NOVALUES useful? Use it when values are unnecessary, reducing the response data needed to enumerate hash fields.

keyPoints: The command takes a hash key and cursor, with optional MATCH, COUNT, and NOVALUES modifiers.
Initialize the scan with cursor 0 and continue with the cursor returned by Redis.
If COUNT is omitted, Redis uses 10 as the default iteration-size hint.
The reply has two top-level parts: the next cursor and the scanned results.
Normal results contain hash fields and their values as pairs.
Each individual HSCAN call has constant time complexity; completing a full iteration is O(N).
gotchas: MATCH filters field names using glob-style matching; it does not perform a general-purpose search.
COUNT is only a per-iteration hint, so a call may return fewer or more fields than requested.
Do not depend on the order of returned fields; collect or sort results when ordering matters.
NOVALUES changes the response shape by omitting values, so consumers must handle fields rather than field/value pairs.

HSET.summary: Creates or updates one or more fields in a Redis hash. It returns how many fields were newly added, excluding fields whose existing values were overwritten.
HSET.explanation: HSET writes one or more field-value pairs into the hash stored at a key. Existing fields are overwritten; if the key does not exist, Redis creates a new hash. The integer reply counts only fields that were newly added, not fields whose existing values were changed.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The Redis key containing the target hash.

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: The first hash field to set.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value assigned to the first field.

parameters.name: [field value ...]
parameters.description: Optional additional field-value pairs, repeated as needed.

HSET.returns: An integer equal to the number of fields newly added to the hash; updates to existing fields are not counted.

example.title: Create and inspect a hash
example.code:
HSET user:42 name "Ada" role "engineer"
HGETALL user:42
example.explanation: Creates or updates two fields, then reads the complete hash.

useCases.title: Model flat records
useCases.scenario: Store a compact record under one Redis key.

useCases.title: Partial updates
useCases.scenario: Change selected attributes without replacing the whole hash.

useCases.title: Multi-field writes
useCases.scenario: Initialize several related attributes in one command.

interview.question: What does HSET return?
interview.answer: HSET stores field-value pairs in a Redis hash and returns the number of fields that were newly created. Updating an existing field returns zero for that field, so the reply is not the total number of pairs written.
interview.followUp: How can several fields be written atomically from the command interface? Supply multiple field-value pairs in one HSET invocation; the command accepts repeated pairs after the first one.

interview.question: What happens when the target key does not exist?
interview.answer: If the key is absent, HSET creates a key containing a hash. If the key already contains a hash, the specified fields are added or modified.
interview.followUp: What should be checked when the key has another Redis data type? The command cannot operate on that incompatible type and should be treated as a wrong-type error.

interview.question: What is the HSET syntax?
interview.answer: The command accepts a key followed by one field and value, with optional additional field-value pairs. Its syntax is `HSET key field value [field value ...]`.
interview.followUp: Which command retrieves one field after writing it? HGET reads the value associated with a specified hash field.

keyPoints: Use HSET to add a field to a hash or change the value associated with an existing field.
The command maps each supplied field to the value immediately following it.
Repeated writes to the same field are replacement operations rather than merges.
gotchas: A missing key is initialized automatically as a hash.
Arguments must consist of at least one field-value pair; additional pairs can be supplied in the same command.

HVALS.summary: Returns all values stored in a Redis hash. Use it when field names are unnecessary; the result order is not guaranteed.
HVALS.explanation: HVALS reads the hash identified by key and returns the values of every field as an array. It does not return field names; use HGETALL when both fields and values are needed.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the hash.

HVALS.returns: An array containing all values in the hash; an absent key returns an empty array.

example.title: Read all hash values
example.code:
HSET myhash field1 "Hello"
HSET myhash field2 "World"
HVALS myhash
example.explanation: Stores two fields in a hash, then returns their values.

useCases.title: Extract hash values
useCases.scenario: An application needs every cached attribute value from a hash but does not need the attribute names.

useCases.title: Batch-read cached values
useCases.scenario: A service prepares a list of cached values for processing or display.

useCases.title: Order-independent verification
useCases.scenario: A test compares the contents of a hash independent of Redis's unspecified iteration order.

interview.question: What does HVALS return, and what is its complexity?
interview.answer: HVALS takes one hash key and returns all values stored in that hash. Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of hash fields.
interview.followUp: How would you retrieve field names as well? Use HGETALL, which returns both fields and values.

interview.question: What is the syntax and behavior for a missing key?
interview.answer: The command is `HVALS key`. The key must identify a hash; the result is an array of values, and an absent key produces an empty array.
interview.followUp: What should be done before calling HVALS if a key might contain another data type? Check or enforce the key's type, because a wrong type causes a Redis error.

interview.question: When should an application use HVALS instead of HGET?
interview.answer: HVALS is useful when only the values from a hash are needed, such as collecting cached record attributes without transferring field names. It is a read-only hash command.
interview.followUp: When would HGET be preferable? Use HGET when one known field is needed, avoiding a full O(N) scan.

keyPoints: HVALS retrieves every value from the hash named by the supplied key, without returning field names.
Its required argument is the key whose value is a Redis hash.
The command is read-only and does not modify the hash.
Execution cost grows linearly with the number of fields in the hash.
Redis classifies HVALS as a read operation on hashes and marks it as slow relative to constant-time commands.

INCR.summary: Increments the integer stored at a key by one. A missing key starts at zero, so the first call returns one.
INCR.explanation: INCR reads the string stored at key as a signed integer, adds one, stores the result back, and returns the new value. If the key is missing, Redis treats it as zero first. The operation is atomic and works in constant time, but fails when the existing value is not a valid integer string or exceeds the signed 64-bit range.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key whose integer value is incremented.

INCR.returns: The new integer value after incrementing, returned as an integer reply; an error is returned for an invalid type or non-integer-representable string.

example.title: Increment a page-view counter
example.code: redis-cli INCR page_views
example.explanation: Atomically increments the counter and prints its new integer value; a missing key starts at zero and therefore returns 1 on the first call.

useCases.title: Event counters
useCases.scenario: Track page views, jobs, logins, or other event totals.

useCases.title: Sequence generation
useCases.scenario: Assign sequential numbers to requests or generated items.

useCases.title: Atomic unit increments
useCases.scenario: Maintain simple per-key quantities that change one unit at a time.

interview.question: What does INCR do when its key does not exist?
interview.answer: INCR atomically adds one to the integer represented by a string key and returns the resulting value. A missing key is treated as zero, so the first increment returns one.
interview.followUp: What happens when the key contains a list? Redis returns a wrong-type error because INCR operates on string values, not list values.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of INCR, and why is it useful for counters?
interview.answer: The command has O(1) time complexity. It updates the value in one Redis command, making it suitable for counters that need atomic increments.
interview.followUp: How would you increment by an arbitrary integer? Use INCRBY with the key and the desired increment.

interview.question: What value formats can INCR process?
interview.answer: INCR parses the stored string as a signed integer, increments it by one, stores the new integer as the key's value, and returns that integer. Values must fit within the signed 64-bit range.
interview.followUp: How can a fractional counter be changed? Use INCRBYFLOAT, which is the related command for floating-point increments.

keyPoints: INCR increases the integer value associated with the specified key by exactly one.
A missing key is initialized to zero before the increment, so the resulting value is one.
The supported numeric range is the signed 64-bit integer range.
Redis categorizes INCR as a write command for string values with fast performance.
A common use is maintaining counters by issuing INCR whenever an event occurs.
gotchas: The key must contain an integer-representable string value; other data types and non-integer strings produce an error.
The counter cannot exceed the signed 64-bit integer range.

INCRBY.summary: INCRBY adds an integer increment to a key's integer value and returns the updated value. Missing keys begin at zero, while wrong types, non-integer strings, and out-of-range values cause errors.
INCRBY.explanation: INCRBY adds a signed integer increment to the integer value held by a key and returns the resulting value. A missing key is treated as zero before the addition; invalid types, non-integer strings, and values outside the signed 64-bit range produce errors.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

parameters.name: increment
parameters.description: The integer amount to add to the value.

INCRBY.returns: Integer reply: the value of the key after the increment.

example.title: Increment a counter
example.code:
redis> SET mykey "10"
OK
redis> INCRBY mykey 5
(integer) 15
example.explanation: Adds 5 to the integer stored in mykey and returns the updated value.

useCases.title: Counters
useCases.scenario: Maintain a request, job, or event total that changes by an arbitrary integer amount.

useCases.title: Decrements
useCases.scenario: Apply a negative increment to reduce a stored integer.

useCases.title: Lazy initialization
useCases.scenario: Create a counter lazily without initializing it first.

interview.question: What does INCRBY do when the key does not exist?
interview.answer: INCRBY atomically adds the supplied integer to the integer stored at the key and returns the new value. If the key is absent, Redis first treats it as zero.
interview.followUp: What happens when the key contains a list? Redis returns a wrong-type error because INCRBY requires an integer-compatible string value.

interview.question: What is the command syntax and return value?
interview.answer: The command takes a key and an integer increment: INCRBY key increment. Its return is an integer reply containing the value after the increment.
interview.followUp: How would you decrement a counter? Supply a negative increment, provided the resulting value remains within the supported signed 64-bit range.

interview.question: What constraints apply to the stored value and result?
interview.answer: INCRBY works with signed 64-bit integers and rejects values that cannot be represented as integers. It also rejects keys containing values of the wrong Redis type.
interview.followUp: What value is returned after a successful update? Redis returns the key's value after applying the increment, rather than the increment itself.

keyPoints: Adds the specified integer amount to the number stored under the key.
A missing key starts at zero, so the first INCRBY can create a counter.
The increment argument is the integer quantity applied to the stored value.
A successful call returns the updated counter value.
Both the stored integer and resulting arithmetic are constrained to signed 64-bit integers.
gotchas: The target must hold a Redis string representing an integer; other Redis types cause an error.
Numeric text must be representable as an integer, not arbitrary numeric or floating-point text.
The operation cannot represent results outside the signed 64-bit integer range.

INCRBYFLOAT.summary: Adds a floating-point number to the numeric string stored at a Redis key and returns the updated value as a string. Missing keys start at zero, and negative increments decrement the value.
INCRBYFLOAT.explanation: INCRBYFLOAT parses the string stored at a key as a double-precision floating-point number, adds the supplied increment, stores the new value back at the same key, and returns that value as a string. A missing key starts at zero; a negative increment performs subtraction.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

parameters.name: increment
parameters.description: The floating-point amount to add to the value. A negative value decrements the value instead.

INCRBYFLOAT.returns: Bulk string reply containing the value of the key after the increment.

example.title: Increment and decrement a Redis string value
example.code:
redis-cli SET mykey 10.50
redis-cli INCRBYFLOAT mykey 0.1
# "10.6"
redis-cli INCRBYFLOAT mykey -5
# "5.6"
example.explanation: The command adds 0.1, then subtracts 5 by using a negative increment.

useCases.title: Atomic floating-point counters
useCases.scenario: Maintain a decimal-valued counter such as a score, balance, or measurement without client-side read-modify-write logic.

useCases.title: Decrementing decimal values
useCases.scenario: Apply a reduction using a negative increment while retaining the same command and key representation.

useCases.title: Server-side numeric updates
useCases.scenario: Update a shared numeric value with one Redis command so competing clients do not need separate GET and SET steps.

interview.question: What does INCRBYFLOAT do when the key does not exist?
interview.answer: It adds the floating-point increment to the value at key and returns the resulting value as a string. If the key is absent, Redis initializes it to zero first.
interview.followUp: What does a negative increment do? It decrements the stored value, because the operation is ordinary addition with a negative operand.

interview.question: What are the syntax and validation requirements?
interview.answer: The syntax is INCRBYFLOAT key increment. Both the existing value and increment must be parseable as double-precision floating-point numbers, and the key must hold a string.
interview.followUp: What is the complexity? The command runs in O(1), as documented in the Redis command reference.

interview.question: What does the command return, and how is the result represented?
interview.answer: On success, Redis stores the updated number at the key and returns it as a bulk string. The returned formatting uses fixed precision of 17 digits after the decimal point.
interview.followUp: How is it persisted and replicated? Redis propagates it as a SET operation to avoid inconsistencies from differing floating-point implementations.

keyPoints: Adds the specified floating-point increment to a numeric string stored at the key.
A missing key is treated as zero before addition.
Negative increments support decrementing without a separate command.
Success replaces the old string with the newly calculated value.
The response is the post-increment value, returned as a bulk string.
Redis propagates and appends the resulting state as SET for deterministic behavior.
gotchas: The command fails when the key contains a non-string value or when either the stored value or increment cannot be parsed as a double-precision floating-point number.
Do not assume the textual result reflects the exact internal precision; output formatting is fixed to 17 digits after the decimal point.
Replication and AOF represent the operation as SET, rather than preserving the original INCRBYFLOAT command.

KEYS.summary: Returns every key name matching a glob-style pattern. Because it can block the Redis server while producing the complete result, reserve it for debugging and exceptional administrative tasks.
KEYS.explanation: KEYS scans the database for every key name matching a glob-style pattern and returns the matches as an array. Pattern characters can select exact names, prefixes, suffixes, or single-character variations, but the command runs synchronously and can block the server while collecting results.

parameters.name: pattern
parameters.description: A glob-style pattern used to match key names.

KEYS.returns: An array reply containing all key names that match the pattern.

example.title: Find keys by prefix
example.code:
redis-cli SET user:1 Alice
redis-cli SET user:2 Bob
redis-cli KEYS 'user:*'
example.explanation: Creates two sample keys, then lists keys whose names begin with user:.

useCases.title: Debug key naming
useCases.scenario: Inspecting a development database

useCases.title: Special keyspace operations
useCases.scenario: Renaming or restructuring a keyspace during maintenance

useCases.title: Targeted inspection
useCases.scenario: Checking whether keys with a naming prefix exist

interview.question: What does the KEYS command do?
interview.answer: KEYS takes one glob-style pattern and returns every key name matching it. For example, KEYS user:* matches keys whose names begin with user:.
interview.followUp: Why can KEYS harm latency? It blocks the Redis server while all matching keys are returned, so large databases can experience substantial pauses.

interview.question: How is KEYS pattern matching specified?
interview.answer: The pattern is the required argument and uses glob-style matching. A literal pattern matches one name, while wildcard patterns can match groups of names.
interview.followUp: What should replace KEYS for incremental traversal? SCAN is the documented alternative when iterating through a keyspace subset because it avoids requesting the entire result at once.

interview.question: When is KEYS appropriate?
interview.answer: KEYS is intended for debugging and special operations, such as changing keyspace layout. It should not be used in regular application code because it can block the server.
interview.followUp: How should a production application find a subset of keys? Prefer SCAN or an appropriate set-based design instead of scanning the full keyspace with KEYS.

keyPoints: The command returns matching key names rather than their values or metadata.
Its sole required argument is a glob-style pattern applied to key names.
Redis classifies KEYS as a keyspace read command that is slow and potentially dangerous.
A match can produce multiple keys, including an empty result when no name fits.
gotchas: Avoid KEYS on large databases or in latency-sensitive application paths because it blocks the server until the complete result is available.
Use it for debugging or exceptional keyspace operations rather than normal application logic.
Cluster deployments may not provide the same keyspace behavior as standalone Redis; consult the cluster guidance before relying on the result.

LPOP.summary: Removes and returns elements from the beginning of a Redis list. It removes one element by default or up to count elements when count is supplied.
LPOP.explanation: LPOP removes elements from the beginning of the list stored at the specified key and returns what it removed. Without count it removes one element; with count it removes up to that many elements, limited by the list length.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the list.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: The maximum number of elements to pop; omitted means one.

LPOP.returns: Without count, a bulk string containing the first element, or nil if the key does not exist. With count, an array containing up to count elements, or nil if the key does not exist.

example.title: Pop list elements from the left
example.code:
RPUSH tasks "build" "test" "deploy"
LPOP tasks
LPOP tasks 2
example.explanation: Adds three values, removes the oldest value, then removes up to two remaining values from the list.

useCases.title: FIFO queue consumption
useCases.scenario: Consume queued work in insertion order by appending with RPUSH and removing with LPOP.

useCases.title: Stack-style processing
useCases.scenario: Use LPUSH and LPOP together when processing the newest item first.

useCases.title: Batch consumption
useCases.scenario: Remove several ready items in one command when batch size is bounded by count.

interview.question: What does LPOP do, and what does count change?
interview.answer: LPOP removes and returns the first element of a list. With count omitted it returns one bulk string; with count supplied it returns up to count elements.
interview.followUp: How does the command behave when count exceeds the list length? It returns every remaining element, not an error.

interview.question: What is LPOP's time complexity?
interview.answer: The command operates on one list key and removes elements from its head. Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of elements returned.
interview.followUp: What alternative supports multiple candidate keys? LMPOP can pop from the first non-empty list among supplied keys.

interview.question: What happens for a missing key or an emptied list?
interview.answer: If the key does not exist, LPOP returns a nil reply. If the last element is popped, Redis removes the list key.
interview.followUp: How can a consumer wait for work instead of polling? BLPOP blocks the connection while the specified lists are empty.

keyPoints: LPOP atomically removes values from the list head and returns those values.
Omitting count makes the command remove exactly one element when available.
With count, the result contains no more than the requested number of elements.
If fewer elements exist than requested, Redis returns only the elements present.
The required key argument identifies the list to modify.
The optional count argument controls the maximum number removed.
Runtime grows with the number of elements returned.
gotchas: When the final list element is removed, Redis deletes the key.
A nonexistent key returns a nil reply rather than an empty list.

LPUSH.summary: LPUSH prepends one or more elements to a Redis list, creating the list when the key is absent. It returns the list's length after insertion.
LPUSH.explanation: LPUSH prepends one or more values to the list at the specified key. Redis creates the key as a list when it is absent; multiple arguments are inserted sequentially, so the rightmost supplied value becomes the first list item.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Name of the key that holds the list.

parameters.name: element [element ...]
parameters.description: One or more values to prepend to the list.

LPUSH.returns: Integer reply: the length of the list after the push operation.

example.title: Prepend values to a list
example.code:
LPUSH mylist "world"
LPUSH mylist "hello"
LRANGE mylist 0 -1
example.explanation: Adds two values at the list head, then reads the complete list to show the newest value first.

useCases.title: Recent-item feeds
useCases.scenario: Add newest items at the front of a list while retaining insertion history.

useCases.title: Queue production
useCases.scenario: Place work identifiers onto a list for later consumption by a worker.

useCases.title: LIFO stacks
useCases.scenario: Build stack-like behavior by pairing head insertion with head removal.

interview.question: What does LPUSH do and what does it return?
interview.answer: LPUSH adds one or more elements to the head of a list and returns the list's length afterward. If the key is absent, Redis creates the list automatically.
interview.followUp: How does LPUSH mylist a b c order the values? The resulting order is c, b, a because arguments are inserted one at a time from left to right at the head.

interview.question: What is the syntax and argument structure of LPUSH?
interview.answer: Its syntax is LPUSH key element [element ...]. The command accepts one or more elements, and the key identifies the target list.
interview.followUp: What happens when the key contains a string? Redis returns a type error because the existing value is not a list.

interview.question: What is LPUSH's complexity?
interview.answer: LPUSH has constant-time complexity for each element added, so a call adding multiple elements takes time proportional to the number of supplied elements. It is categorized as a write operation on a list.
interview.followUp: Which command provides the create-only-if-present behavior? LPUSHX prepends values only when the key already exists and contains a list.

keyPoints: LPUSH prepends every supplied element to the target list.
An absent key is initialized as an empty list before insertion.
The result is the list length after all insertions complete.
Each individual element insertion has constant-time complexity.
Redis classifies LPUSH as a write command for list data structures and marks it fast.
gotchas: The command fails if the key already contains a non-list value.
With multiple elements, insertion order is reversed in the resulting list: the last argument ends up at the head.

LRANGE.summary: Returns an inclusive range of elements from a Redis list. Start and stop use zero-based indexes, and negative indexes count from the list's tail.
LRANGE.explanation: LRANGE reads the elements between the supplied zero-based start and stop positions from a Redis list. Both boundaries are inclusive, negative positions count backward from the tail, and indexes outside the list are tolerated rather than treated as errors.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Name of the key that holds the list.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: Zero-based starting index; negative indexes count from the tail.

parameters.name: stop
parameters.description: Inclusive zero-based ending index; negative indexes count from the tail.

LRANGE.returns: An array containing the selected list elements, or an empty array if the key does not exist.

example.title: Read a complete Redis list
example.code:
redis-cli RPUSH mylist one two three
redis-cli LRANGE mylist 0 -1
# 1) "one"
# 2) "two"
# 3) "three"
example.explanation: Adds three values, then reads the entire list with an inclusive range from the first element through the last.

useCases.title: List retrieval and pagination
useCases.scenario: Read all values in a list with 0 -1 or fetch a bounded slice for display.

useCases.title: Recent-item inspection
useCases.scenario: Inspect the newest entries by using a negative range such as -5 -1.

useCases.title: Queue monitoring
useCases.scenario: Read a queue segment without removing its jobs.

interview.question: How do LRANGE indexes work?
interview.answer: LRANGE returns a selected portion of a list using zero-based start and stop indexes. The stop index is inclusive, so 0 0 reads the first element and 0 -1 reads the whole list.
interview.followUp: How does it behave when indexes exceed the list? Out-of-range indexes do not cause errors; the result contains the overlapping elements, or is empty when the range does not overlap.

interview.question: What do negative indexes mean in LRANGE?
interview.answer: Negative indexes count from the tail: -1 identifies the last element, -2 the previous one, and so forth. This makes 0 -1 a convenient full-list read.
interview.followUp: What happens if the key is absent? Redis returns an empty array.

interview.question: What is LRANGE's time complexity?
interview.answer: The command has O(S+N) complexity, where S is the distance from the relevant list end to the start offset and N is the number of returned elements. Reading a large range therefore costs more than reading a small one.
interview.followUp: Which list operation can prepare the example list? RPUSH appends values to the list, after which LRANGE can read them.

keyPoints: LRANGE selects and returns elements from the list associated with the specified key.
Both positions use zero-based indexing, with the first list element at position zero.
The stop boundary is included in the returned range.
A negative position measures backward from the list's final element.
Runtime is O(S+N), combining the traversal distance to the start with the number of returned items.
gotchas: Indexes beyond the list boundaries are accepted; they simply select whatever portion overlaps the list.
A start position after the list's end produces no elements.
A missing key returns an empty array rather than an error.

MGET.summary: MGET atomically retrieves the string values of one or more keys in a single command. Missing keys and keys holding non-string values return nil in their corresponding result positions.
MGET.explanation: MGET atomically reads the string values for one or more keys and returns them as an array aligned with the requested key order. A missing key or a key containing a non-string value contributes nil, so the command does not fail for those cases.

parameters.name: key [key ...]
parameters.description: One or more keys whose string values should be retrieved.

MGET.returns: An array of values corresponding to the specified keys; missing keys and keys that do not hold strings return nil.

example.title: Read several string keys
example.code:
redis-cli SET user:1 Alice
redis-cli SET user:2 Bob
redis-cli MGET user:1 user:2 user:3
example.explanation: The command returns the values in key order; the missing key produces nil.

useCases.title: Batch cache reads
useCases.scenario: Read several cached string fields in one request.

useCases.title: Lower read latency
useCases.scenario: Fetch a group of independent values while reducing client-server round trips.

useCases.title: Aligned multi-key results
useCases.scenario: Preserve the association between requested keys and returned values by using the response positions.

interview.question: What does MGET do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: MGET accepts one or more keys and returns an array containing the corresponding values. Results preserve the input-key order, and missing or non-string keys contribute nil.
interview.followUp: What is its time complexity? It is O(N), where N is the number of keys retrieved.

interview.question: Why use MGET instead of issuing several GET commands?
interview.answer: MGET is atomic as a command: Redis returns the string values for all requested keys in one operation. It is useful when several independent string values must be read with fewer client-server round trips.
interview.followUp: How would you reduce latency further for many unrelated requests? Compare MGET with pipelining, while considering the key distribution and the deployment's clustering behavior.

interview.question: What happens when one requested key is missing or has the wrong type?
interview.answer: MGET is intended for string values. If a requested key is absent or does not contain a string, its position in the returned array is nil rather than causing the whole command to fail.
interview.followUp: How should an application distinguish an absent key from a non-string key? Use an additional type-aware check such as TYPE when that distinction matters, because MGET itself reports nil for both cases.

keyPoints: Use MGET to retrieve multiple Redis string values in one atomic command.
The response contains one result for every supplied key.
Missing keys and non-string keys do not abort the complete multi-key read.
Redis classifies MGET as a read operation for string data and marks it fast.
Execution cost grows linearly with the number of requested keys.
gotchas: A missing key and a key with a non-string data type both produce nil, which can make those cases indistinguishable from the returned value alone.
Cluster configuration affects multi-key behavior; verify the documented clustering rules before assuming every requested key is handled identically.

MSET.summary: MSET atomically assigns string values to one or more keys in a single command. Existing values are overwritten, and a successful command returns OK.
MSET.explanation: MSET accepts one or more key-value pairs and writes every pair as a single atomic operation. Existing values are replaced, and the command returns OK when the operation completes successfully.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: A key whose string value will be written.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The string value assigned to the preceding key.

parameters.name: key value ...
parameters.description: Additional key-value pairs; at least one pair is required.

example.title: Set multiple string keys
example.code:
MSET user:1 Alice user:2 Bob
GET user:1
GET user:2
example.explanation: Stores two string values in one command, then reads them back.

useCases.title: Batch cache population
useCases.scenario: Write several related cache entries while reducing client-server round trips.

useCases.title: Atomic multi-key update
useCases.scenario: Replace a group of string values so readers see either the old or complete new state.

useCases.title: Bulk initialization
useCases.scenario: Initialize multiple independent string keys in one request.

interview.question: What does MSET do, and is it atomic?
interview.answer: MSET writes multiple string key-value pairs in one command and replaces values that already exist. It is atomic, so clients cannot observe only part of the batch.
interview.followUp: How does its complexity scale? It is O(N), where N is the number of keys being set.

interview.question: What is MSET's syntax and return value?
interview.answer: The command takes alternating keys and values: MSET key value [key value ...]. It returns the simple string reply OK because the command cannot fail under its documented conditions.
interview.followUp: What would you use to avoid overwriting existing keys? MSETNX, which provides conditional multi-key creation.

interview.question: What should you consider when using MSET with Redis Cluster?
interview.answer: MSET is useful for reducing round trips when several string values must be written together. In clustered deployments, however, its multi-key behavior varies, so key placement must be considered.
interview.followUp: What cluster constraint should be investigated? Whether the participating keys can be handled together according to Redis cluster multi-key operation rules.

keyPoints: MSET writes each supplied key with its corresponding string value.
If a key already exists, its previous value is replaced.
The complete batch becomes visible atomically rather than as separate updates.
Readers cannot observe a partially applied MSET batch.
Execution cost grows linearly with the number of key-value pairs.
A successful invocation returns OK.
gotchas: In clustered Redis, multi-key behavior can differ; consult the multi-key operations guidance when keys may be distributed across hash slots.
MSET overwrites existing values; use MSETNX when conditional, no-overwrite behavior is required.

MULTI.summary: MULTI starts a Redis transaction and queues later commands on the current connection. EXEC runs the queued commands atomically, while DISCARD cancels them.
MULTI.explanation: MULTI switches the current connection into transaction mode. Commands sent afterward are queued rather than run immediately, and EXEC later runs the queued commands as one atomic batch; DISCARD can instead clear the queue and leave transaction mode.

example.title: Queue and execute a transaction
example.code:
MULTI
SET cache:user:42 "Ada"
INCR stats:users
EXEC
example.explanation: Starts a transaction, queues two commands, then executes them atomically with EXEC.

useCases.title: Atomic grouped updates
useCases.scenario: Update several related keys as one uninterrupted operation.

useCases.title: Transaction batching
useCases.scenario: Batch commands that must be committed together.

useCases.title: Optimistic concurrency control
useCases.scenario: Pair with WATCH when writes depend on a prior read.

interview.question: What does MULTI do?
interview.answer: MULTI marks the beginning of a Redis transaction and changes the connection into transaction mode. Subsequent commands are queued, and EXEC executes them as a group.
interview.followUp: How can a client cancel the transaction? Send DISCARD; it removes the queued commands and restores the connection to normal mode.

interview.question: What replies should a client expect after MULTI?
interview.answer: MULTI itself returns the simple string reply OK. Commands issued after MULTI normally return QUEUED because Redis schedules them for execution at EXEC.
interview.followUp: When are the commands' actual results available? EXEC returns the results after the queued commands run.

interview.question: What are MULTI's syntax, complexity, and introduction version?
interview.answer: MULTI has O(1) time complexity and was introduced in Redis Open Source 1.2.0. Its syntax is simply MULTI, with no arguments.
interview.followUp: Which related commands complete or cancel the transaction? EXEC commits the queued commands, while DISCARD aborts them.

keyPoints: MULTI begins a transaction on the current client connection.
Commands after MULTI wait in a queue and are executed together when EXEC is called.
A successful MULTI command acknowledges entry into transaction mode with OK.
EXEC is the commit point that causes Redis to run the queued commands.
The command has no client API method signature documented on its command-reference page.
gotchas: Clustered deployments can impose different transaction behavior, so verify the multi-key transaction constraints for the topology in use.
Do not expect queued commands to return their normal results before EXEC; their immediate replies indicate that they were queued.
Use DISCARD to abandon the queued commands instead of executing them.

PERSIST.summary: Removes the existing expiration from a key, making it persistent. Returns 1 when a timeout was removed, otherwise 0.
PERSIST.explanation: PERSIST removes the expiration associated with a key. The key remains present and becomes persistent; the command reports whether an expiration was actually removed.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

PERSIST.returns: Integer reply: 1 if the timeout has been removed; 0 if the key does not exist or does not have an associated timeout.

example.title: Remove a key expiration
example.code:
redis-cli SET session:123 "active"
redis-cli EXPIRE session:123 300
redis-cli PERSIST session:123
redis-cli TTL session:123
example.explanation: The final TTL is -1, showing that the key no longer has an expiration.

useCases.title: Promote a cache entry to persistent
useCases.scenario: A cache entry must survive beyond its previously assigned TTL.

useCases.title: Keep selected application state
useCases.scenario: A session or configuration key should remain available indefinitely after a condition is met.

useCases.title: Cancel expiration
useCases.scenario: Application logic needs to cancel a scheduled key expiration.

interview.question: What does PERSIST do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: PERSIST key removes the key's existing timeout, changing it from volatile to persistent. It returns 1 when a timeout was removed and 0 when the key is missing or has no timeout.
interview.followUp: How can you verify the result? Use TTL: it returns -1 for an existing key with no associated timeout.

interview.question: What are PERSIST's complexity and required argument?
interview.answer: The command has O(1) time complexity. It takes one required argument, key, which identifies the key whose expiration should be removed.
interview.followUp: What is the command syntax? PERSIST key.

interview.question: Does PERSIST delete or modify the key's value?
interview.answer: PERSIST changes expiration metadata; it does not delete the key or alter its value. After successful removal, the key remains available without an associated timeout.
interview.followUp: What happens if the key already has no timeout? The command returns 0 and leaves that state unchanged.

keyPoints: PERSIST removes the current expiration and makes the key persistent.
Once its timeout is removed, the key will not expire because it has no associated timeout.
A return value of 1 confirms that PERSIST removed the timeout.
The command returns 0 when the named key is absent.
PERSIST completes in constant time.
Its required argument is the key name whose expiration should be removed.
gotchas: A return value of 0 does not distinguish between a missing key and an existing key without an expiration.

PEXPIRE.summary: Sets a key's expiration timeout in milliseconds. Optional NX, XX, GT, and LT modes conditionally control whether the timeout is applied.
PEXPIRE.explanation: PEXPIRE assigns a timeout to an existing key in milliseconds. Redis removes the key after the timeout elapses; optional mutually exclusive modes restrict setting the expiry based on whether an expiry exists or how the new timeout compares with the current one.
PEXPIRE.syntax: PEXPIRE key milliseconds [NX | XX | GT | LT]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Key whose timeout is modified.

parameters.name: milliseconds
parameters.description: Timeout duration, in milliseconds.

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: Optional mutually exclusive condition: NX, XX, GT, or LT.

PEXPIRE.returns: Integer reply: 1 if the timeout was set; 0 if it was not set, including when the key does not exist or an option condition fails.

example.title: Set a millisecond expiration
example.code:
SET session:42 "active"
PEXPIRE session:42 1500
PTTL session:42
example.explanation: Stores a value, assigns a 1.5-second expiration, then reads the remaining lifetime in milliseconds.

useCases.title: Apply precise cache expiration
useCases.scenario: Session and cache entries need sub-second or exact millisecond lifetimes.

useCases.title: Conditionally initialize a timeout
useCases.scenario: A write should establish an expiry only if another operation has not already set one.

useCases.title: Adjust an existing expiration
useCases.scenario: A refresh should extend or shorten an existing lifetime only under a chosen comparison.

interview.question: What does PEXPIRE do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: PEXPIRE sets a key's time-to-live using milliseconds rather than seconds. It returns 1 when the timeout is applied and 0 when it is not, such as when the key does not exist.
interview.followUp: How would you verify millisecond precision? Use PTTL after setting the timeout; it reports the remaining lifetime in milliseconds.

interview.question: Explain the NX, XX, GT, and LT options.
interview.answer: NX applies the timeout only if the key currently has no expiry, while XX requires an existing expiry. GT applies it only when the new timeout is greater than the current one, and LT requires it to be less.
interview.followUp: What happens if these modes are combined? The options are mutually exclusive, so they must be supplied individually.

interview.question: When is an expired key removed and when are expiration events generated?
interview.answer: A positive timeout causes the key to expire after the specified duration. Redis can remove expired keys when accessed or through background expiration, so expiration-related events are not guaranteed to occur exactly when the TTL reaches zero.
interview.followUp: What event accompanies a negative timeout? Redis deletes the key immediately and emits only a del event, rather than an expire event.

keyPoints: PEXPIRE is the millisecond-granularity counterpart of EXPIRE.
The key argument identifies the key whose lifetime should be changed.
The milliseconds argument specifies the duration before expiration.
NX protects an already-expiring key by applying the timeout only when no expiry exists.
XX requires the target key to already have an expiration.
GT allows replacement only when the new expiration is later than the current expiration.
LT allows replacement only when the new expiration is earlier than the current expiration.
gotchas: NX, XX, GT, and LT cannot be combined.
With GT, a key without an expiry is considered to have an infinite current TTL, so a finite new expiry does not replace it.
A missing key or a condition that fails returns 0 rather than applying an expiry.

PTTL.summary: Returns the remaining expiration time of a key in milliseconds. It distinguishes an existing key without expiration (-1) from a missing key (-2).
PTTL.explanation: PTTL takes one key and reports how long that key will remain before expiration, measured in milliseconds. A nonnegative result is the remaining lifetime; -1 distinguishes an existing key without expiration from -2, which means the key does not exist.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key whose remaining expiration should be returned.

PTTL.returns: An integer: the remaining TTL in milliseconds; -1 if the key exists without an associated expiration; or -2 if the key does not exist.

example.title: Inspect a millisecond expiration
example.code:
SET session:42 "user-123" PX 30000
PTTL session:42
example.explanation: Stores a session with a 30-second millisecond expiration, then reads its remaining lifetime.

useCases.title: Read cache freshness
useCases.scenario: A cache client needs to expose or calculate how long a cached entry remains valid with millisecond precision.

useCases.title: Calculate retry timing
useCases.scenario: A rate limiter needs the remaining lockout interval to tell a client when retrying may be reasonable.

useCases.title: Inspect key lifecycle
useCases.scenario: An operations check verifies whether a key has an expiration and observes its remaining duration.

interview.question: What does PTTL measure, and how does it differ from TTL?
interview.answer: PTTL returns the remaining time to live for a key in milliseconds. Unlike TTL, which reports seconds, PTTL uses millisecond units.
interview.followUp: How would you distinguish a missing key from a persistent key? Check for -2 for a missing key and -1 for an existing key without an expiration.

interview.question: What are PTTL's argument and time complexity?
interview.answer: The command accepts one required argument: the key whose expiration is being inspected. Its time complexity is O(1), making the lookup constant time.
interview.followUp: What should a caller do when the result is nonnegative? Treat it as the remaining lifetime in milliseconds, while remembering that it can decrease immediately after the read.

interview.question: What values can PTTL return?
interview.answer: PTTL returns an integer reply: a nonnegative TTL in milliseconds, -1 when the key exists without an expiration, or -2 when the key does not exist. These meanings apply to both RESP2 and RESP3.
interview.followUp: Which command can establish a millisecond expiration before checking it? PEXPIRE sets a relative timeout with millisecond precision.

keyPoints: PTTL reports a key's remaining expiration interval using milliseconds.
The required key argument identifies which Redis key to inspect.
Use PTTL when millisecond units are needed; TTL provides the corresponding value in seconds.
The command has been available since Redis Open Source 2.6.0.
PTTL performs a constant-time expiration lookup.
gotchas: Do not interpret every negative result as the same condition: -2 means the key is absent.
An existing persistent key returns -1, so callers should handle it separately from a missing key.

PUBLISH.summary: PUBLISH sends a message to a channel for delivery to its current subscribers. It returns the number of clients that received the message.
PUBLISH.explanation: PUBLISH sends a message to every client currently subscribed to the specified channel. In a Redis Cluster, Redis forwards the publication as needed, but the returned count includes only clients connected to the publisher's node.

parameters.name: channel
parameters.description: Channel to publish the message to.

parameters.name: message
parameters.description: Message to publish.

PUBLISH.returns: Integer reply: the number of clients that the message was sent to.

example.title: Publish to a channel
example.code:
redis-cli SUBSCRIBE news
redis-cli PUBLISH news "Redis update"
example.explanation: Run the subscriber in one terminal and the publisher in another; the publisher receives the number of clients that received the message.

useCases.title: Real-time notifications
useCases.scenario: Broadcast an event to all currently connected consumers of a topic.

useCases.title: Job completion signaling
useCases.scenario: Signal a waiting service that an operation completed without polling.

useCases.title: Event fan-out
useCases.scenario: Fan out a serialized application event to active listeners.

interview.question: What does PUBLISH do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: PUBLISH takes a channel and a message, then returns an integer representing the number of clients that received it. The command does not require subscribers to exist.
interview.followUp: How does this count behave in a cluster? It includes only clients connected to the same node as the publishing client.

interview.question: What are PUBLISH's arguments?
interview.answer: The command uses the syntax `PUBLISH channel message`. The channel identifies the publication topic, while the message is the payload delivered to subscribers.
interview.followUp: How can clients receive pattern-based publications? They can use PSUBSCRIBE; Redis sends those deliveries as pattern-matching messages.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of PUBLISH?
interview.answer: PUBLISH has time complexity O(N+M), where N is the number of clients subscribed to the receiving channel and M is the total number of subscribed patterns.
interview.followUp: What delivery guarantee does Redis Pub/Sub provide? At-most-once delivery: a message is delivered once if at all.

keyPoints: PUBLISH broadcasts the supplied payload on one named channel.
Cluster clients may issue PUBLISH against any node.
Redis Cluster routes publications so subscribers can connect through any node.
The integer response reports how many clients received the publication.
Its cost grows with direct subscribers and subscribed patterns.
PUBLISH has been available since Redis Open Source 2.0.0.
gotchas: In a Redis Cluster, the integer reply does not count subscribers connected to other nodes.

RENAME.summary: Renames a key to a new name, replacing the destination if it already exists. In Redis Cluster, both names must belong to the same hash slot.
RENAME.explanation: RENAME moves an existing key from key to newkey and returns success. If the destination already exists, Redis replaces it; in clustered deployments, both names must map to the same hash slot.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key to rename.

parameters.name: newkey
parameters.description: The new key name. An existing key with this name is overwritten.

RENAME.returns: Simple string: OK on success; an error when the source key does not exist.

example.title: Rename a key
example.code:
SET user:42 "Ada"
RENAME user:42 user:99
GET user:99
example.explanation: Stores a value, moves the key to a new name, then reads it through the new name.

useCases.title: Migrate a key name
useCases.scenario: Change a cache key after a namespace or identifier migration without rewriting its stored value.

useCases.title: Promote staged data
useCases.scenario: Publish a completed temporary value under its final key name.

useCases.title: Cluster-compatible renaming
useCases.scenario: Move a key within a cluster when both names share a hash tag and slot.

interview.question: What does RENAME do when the source key is missing?
interview.answer: RENAME changes the name of an existing key and returns a simple string success response. If the source key does not exist, Redis returns an error.
interview.followUp: What happens when the destination exists? Redis overwrites it through an implicit DEL, which can add latency for a very large value.

interview.question: What is RENAME's time complexity, and what performance caveat applies?
interview.answer: The command has O(1) time complexity in the usual case. However, replacing an existing destination can incur deletion work that is not represented by the nominal rename complexity.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid an unconditional overwrite? Use RENAMENX, which renames only when the target name does not already exist.

interview.question: What restriction applies to RENAME in cluster mode?
interview.answer: In Redis Cluster, the source and destination must be assigned to the same hash slot. Keys using the same hash tag can be designed to satisfy that requirement.
interview.followUp: Why does this matter? Multi-key operations cannot reliably coordinate keys placed in different cluster slots.

keyPoints: The command transfers the key's existing value and associated data to the new name.
A missing source key causes the command to fail rather than creating the destination.
The destination name is not preserved when it already refers to another key.
RENAME has been available since Redis Open Source 1.0.0.
The documented normal-case complexity is constant time.
gotchas: The destination is replaced without a protection check, so use RENAMENX when overwriting an existing destination would be unsafe.
Replacing a large destination can trigger an implicit deletion and add latency.
Cluster deployments require compatible hash slots, typically achieved by using the same hash tag in both names.

RESTORE.summary: RESTORE creates a key by deserializing a serialized value produced by DUMP. It can apply a relative or absolute expiration and optionally replace an existing key or initialize eviction metadata.
RESTORE.explanation: RESTORE deserializes a value produced by DUMP and creates the specified key. A TTL of zero means no expiration; otherwise Redis interprets the TTL as milliseconds, or as an absolute Unix-millisecond expiration time when ABSTTL is supplied.
RESTORE.syntax: RESTORE key ttl serialized-value [REPLACE] [ABSTTL] [IDLETIME seconds] [FREQ frequency]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Name of the destination key to create.

parameters.name: ttl
parameters.description: Expiration in milliseconds; zero means no expiration. With ABSTTL, it is an absolute Unix timestamp in milliseconds.

parameters.name: serialized-value
parameters.description: Serialized value produced by DUMP.

parameters.name: REPLACE
parameters.description: Replace the destination if it exists.

parameters.name: ABSTTL
parameters.description: Interpret ttl as an absolute Unix timestamp in milliseconds.

parameters.name: IDLETIME seconds
parameters.description: Set idle time for LRU eviction, in seconds.

parameters.name: FREQ frequency
parameters.description: Set the access-frequency counter for LFU eviction.

RESTORE.returns: A simple string status reply, normally OK on success; errors are returned for a busy destination without REPLACE or invalid serialized data.

example.title: Copy a serialized key
example.explanation: Serializes one key with DUMP and recreates it under another name with a 60-second relative expiration.

useCases.title: Key migration or duplication
useCases.scenario: Move or copy a value between key names after obtaining its serialized representation with DUMP.

useCases.title: Cache restoration with expiration
useCases.scenario: Recreate cached data while preserving a relative lifetime or supplying an absolute expiration deadline.

useCases.title: Eviction metadata initialization
useCases.scenario: Restore data while initializing idle time or access frequency used by an eviction policy.

interview.question: What does RESTORE do?
interview.answer: RESTORE creates a key by deserializing a serialized value, normally one returned by DUMP. Its TTL argument is expressed in milliseconds, and zero creates the key without expiration.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve an absolute expiration timestamp? Use ABSTTL, which makes the TTL argument an absolute Unix timestamp in milliseconds rather than a relative duration.

interview.question: How do you restore over an existing key?
interview.answer: By default, RESTORE fails when the destination key already exists. REPLACE changes that behavior by replacing the existing key.
interview.followUp: What happens if the destination does not exist but the payload is invalid? Redis validates the RDB version and checksum and returns an error when they do not match.

interview.question: What are IDLETIME and FREQ used for?
interview.answer: IDLETIME sets the restored key's idle time in seconds for LRU eviction, while FREQ sets its access-frequency counter for LFU eviction. These options let restoration initialize eviction-related metadata.
interview.followUp: When should ABSTTL be used instead of a relative TTL? Use it when the expiration is already represented as an absolute Unix timestamp in milliseconds, such as when preserving a shared deadline.

keyPoints: RESTORE reconstructs a Redis key from an opaque serialized representation, typically generated by DUMP.
A zero TTL creates a persistent key rather than applying an expiration.
ABSTTL switches the TTL from a relative duration to an absolute expiration timestamp.
REPLACE allows restoration to overwrite an existing destination key.
IDLETIME initializes the restored key's idle time in seconds for LRU eviction behavior.
FREQ initializes the restored key's access-frequency counter for LFU eviction behavior.
gotchas: An existing destination key causes an error unless REPLACE is included.
Redis rejects payloads when the serialized data's RDB version or checksum validation fails.

RPUSH.summary: Appends one or more values to the tail of a Redis list, creating the key when absent. It returns the list's new length.
RPUSH.explanation: RPUSH appends every supplied element to the right-hand end of the list at key. Redis creates the key as a list when it is absent; arguments are added from left to right, and a non-list value causes an error. The command returns the resulting list length.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the list.

parameters.name: element [element ...]
parameters.description: One or more values to append to the list.

RPUSH.returns: Integer reply: the length of the list after the push operation.

example.title: Append values and inspect the list
example.code:
redis-cli RPUSH mylist "hello" "world"
redis-cli LRANGE mylist 0 -1
example.explanation: Appends two values, then reads the complete list to verify their order.

useCases.title: Build an ordered list
useCases.scenario: Append events, jobs, or records while preserving insertion order.

useCases.title: Implement a queue
useCases.scenario: Add work at the tail and remove it from the head with LPOP or BLPOP.

useCases.title: Batch list appends
useCases.scenario: Add several related values in one command call.

interview.question: What does RPUSH do when its key does not exist?
interview.answer: RPUSH adds one or more values at the tail of a Redis list and returns the list length after the operation. If the key is missing, Redis creates the list first.
interview.followUp: How does a multi-element call affect complexity? Each added element takes constant time, so adding N elements in one call is O(N).

interview.question: Explain RPUSH's arguments and ordering.
interview.answer: The syntax is `RPUSH key element [element ...]`. `key` identifies the list, while the variadic element portion supplies one or more values to append.
interview.followUp: What ordering results from `RPUSH mylist a b c`? The list contains a, then b, then c, because values are appended left to right.

interview.question: What does RPUSH return, and when can it fail?
interview.answer: The command returns an integer representing the list's length after the push. A key containing a non-list value produces an error instead of being converted.
interview.followUp: Which command appends only when the list already exists? `RPUSHX` provides that conditional behavior.

keyPoints: All supplied values are appended to the list's tail.
A missing key is initialized as an empty list before values are added.
One invocation can append multiple values.
Multiple arguments preserve their left-to-right order in the resulting list.
The response is the list's new length.
gotchas: The command fails if the key already contains a non-list value.
With multiple values, their command-line order becomes their list order.

SCAN.summary: SCAN incrementally iterates over key names in the currently selected Redis database. Continue with each returned cursor until it becomes 0, optionally filtering by pattern, count hint, or type.
SCAN.explanation: SCAN incrementally iterates key names in the currently selected database. Each call receives a cursor and returns a new cursor plus a batch of keys; continue until the cursor returns to 0, optionally constraining results with MATCH, COUNT, or TYPE.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: Cursor position; use 0 to begin and the returned cursor for the next call.

parameters.name: MATCH pattern
parameters.description: Optional glob-style pattern used to filter returned key names.

parameters.name: COUNT count
parameters.description: Optional work-count hint for each call; it is not an exact result count.

parameters.name: TYPE type
parameters.description: Optional Redis data type used to restrict returned keys.

SCAN.returns: A two-element array containing the next cursor and an array of key names.

example.title: Iterate matching keys
example.explanation: Starts at cursor 0, repeatedly supplies the returned cursor, filters keys with MATCH, and stops when Redis returns cursor 0.

useCases.title: Incremental keyspace inspection
useCases.scenario: Traverse a large keyspace in bounded batches instead of requesting every key at once.

useCases.title: Pattern-based discovery
useCases.scenario: Find keys belonging to a namespace without using a blocking whole-keyspace command.

useCases.title: Type-restricted maintenance
useCases.scenario: Process only keys whose Redis data type is appropriate for an operation.

interview.question: How do you complete a SCAN iteration?
interview.answer: SCAN iterates keys in the selected database without requiring a key argument. Start with cursor 0, pass each returned cursor into the next call, and finish when it becomes 0.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid scanning keys of the wrong type? Use the optional TYPE argument, while remembering that matching and iteration behavior still apply.

interview.question: What do MATCH and COUNT do?
interview.answer: MATCH accepts a glob-style pattern and limits which returned keys are reported. COUNT suggests how much work Redis should do per call, but it does not guarantee the batch length.
interview.followUp: Why might MATCH return an empty batch? Matching is performed after Redis retrieves elements, so a batch may contain no matching keys.

interview.question: What is SCAN's complexity and what does it imply?
interview.answer: Each call has constant operation complexity, while completing an iteration is O(N), where N is the number of elements in the database. SCAN is therefore suitable for incremental traversal rather than one large blocking result.
interview.followUp: What property must production code handle? Results are not ordered and may repeat, so consumers should tolerate duplicates and avoid relying on order.

keyPoints: SCAN traverses key names in the currently selected Redis database.
Begin with cursor 0 and feed every returned cursor into the following call.
MATCH restricts reported keys to a glob-style pattern.
A call is O(1); a complete traversal is O(N).
gotchas: MATCH can produce empty batches because filtering happens after Redis fetches candidates.

SET.summary: Sets a key to a string, creating it or replacing its current value. Conditions, expiration controls, and GET support conditional writes, lifetimes, and retrieval of the previous string.
SET.explanation: SET writes a string value to a key, creating it when absent or replacing its existing value regardless of the existing type. Optional conditions control whether the write occurs, while expiration options assign or preserve a lifetime; GET can return the previous string value instead of the normal status response.
SET.syntax: SET key value [NX | XX | IFEQ ifeq-value | IFNE ifne-value | IFDEQ ifdeq-digest | IFDNE ifdne-digest] [GET] [EX seconds | PX milliseconds | EXAT unix-time-seconds | PXAT unix-time-milliseconds | KEEPTTL]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Name of the key.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The string value to set.

SET.returns: Without GET, OK on success; with NX or XX when the condition fails, nil; with GET, the old string or nil. An error occurs with GET if the existing value is not a string.

example.title: Conditional write with expiration
example.code:
SET session:user:42 active EX 300 NX
GET session:user:42
example.explanation: Creates the key only when absent and sets a five-minute expiration.

useCases.title: Insert-if-absent initialization
useCases.scenario: Create a value only when no value is present, avoiding an overwrite.

useCases.title: Expiring cache values
useCases.scenario: Attach a lifetime directly to a cache entry during the write.

useCases.title: Conditional updates
useCases.scenario: Replace an existing value only when the key is already present.

interview.question: What does SET do when the key already exists?
interview.answer: SET stores a string at the specified key. It creates a missing key and overwrites an existing value regardless of its type; a successful ordinary write returns OK.
interview.followUp: How can a write be conditional? Use NX for an absent key or XX for an existing key, with the condition options mutually exclusive.

interview.question: How does SET control expiration?
interview.answer: EX and PX specify relative expiration in seconds or milliseconds. EXAT and PXAT specify absolute Unix expiration times, while KEEPTTL preserves the existing lifetime.
interview.followUp: What happens if multiple expiration options are supplied? They are mutually exclusive, so the command must select only one.

interview.question: What does the GET option change?
interview.answer: GET makes SET return the old string stored at the key, or nil when the key did not exist. If the existing value is not a string, Redis returns an error and aborts SET.
interview.followUp: Does GET make SET type-safe for other Redis data types? No; it errors on a non-string existing value rather than converting or replacing it.

keyPoints: SET writes string data even when the key currently contains another Redis data type.
A missing key is created by a successful unconditional SET.
NX turns SET into an insert-only operation.
XX prevents SET from creating a new key.
GET changes the reply to the prior string value, or nil for an absent key.
EX assigns a positive whole-number lifetime measured in seconds.
gotchas: Use at most one condition option in a command.
Expiration options are mutually exclusive; choose one lifetime behavior.
With GET, a non-string existing value causes an error rather than returning it.
A successful overwrite removes the old expiry unless KEEPTTL is used.

SETEX.summary: SETEX stores a string at a key and gives it a timeout in seconds. It is deprecated in favor of SET with the EX option.
SETEX.explanation: SETEX writes a string to the specified key and assigns an expiration measured in seconds. It replaces an existing value and is functionally the same as SET with the EX option; invalid seconds cause an error.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

parameters.name: seconds
parameters.description: The time to live, in seconds.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value to set.

SETEX.returns: Simple string reply: OK when the operation succeeds.

example.title: Cache a value with a timeout
example.code:
redis-cli SETEX cache:user:42 60 '{"name":"Ada"}'
redis-cli TTL cache:user:42
redis-cli GET cache:user:42
example.explanation: Stores a JSON string for 60 seconds, then checks its remaining lifetime and reads the value.

useCases.title: Expiring cache entries
useCases.scenario: Cache a serialized response with a bounded lifetime so stale data disappears automatically.

useCases.title: Temporary credentials
useCases.scenario: Store a short-lived token or session value without requiring a separate expiration command.

useCases.title: Self-expiring coordination data
useCases.scenario: Set a safety timeout on a transient coordination key.

interview.question: What does SETEX do and what is its complexity?
interview.answer: SETEX takes a key, a lifetime in seconds, and a string value. It sets the value and expiration together in one operation, with O(1) complexity.
interview.followUp: How should new code express the same operation? Use SET key value EX seconds, which is the documented replacement.

interview.question: What are SETEX's arguments?
interview.answer: The syntax is SETEX key seconds value. The seconds argument is the key's time to live, and the value is the string stored under the key.
interview.followUp: What happens if seconds is invalid? Redis returns an error rather than applying the command.

interview.question: What happens when the key already exists?
interview.answer: An existing key is overwritten with the supplied string and receives the specified expiration. The command creates the key when it does not already exist.
interview.followUp: How can the remaining lifetime be inspected? Use TTL on the key after SETEX.

keyPoints: SETEX stores a string and schedules the key to expire after the requested number of seconds.
Its behavior can be expressed with SET followed by the EX expiration option.
The key argument identifies the Redis key to create or replace.
The seconds argument specifies how long the key remains available.
The value argument supplies the string stored by the command.
SETEX creates the target key when no key with that name currently exists.
gotchas: SETEX is deprecated; use SET with EX for new code or migrations.
The seconds argument must be valid; otherwise Redis returns an error.

SETNX.summary: Sets a string value only when a key does not already exist. It returns 1 when the key is created and 0 when no write occurs; SET with NX is the recommended replacement for new code.
SETNX.explanation: SETNX attempts to store a string value only when the named key is absent. It performs no write when the key already exists and reports whether the write occurred with an integer result.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value to set, only if the key does not already exist.

SETNX.returns: Integer reply: 1 if the key was set; 0 if the key was not set.

example.title: Set only when absent
example.code:
SETNX mykey "Hello"
SETNX mykey "World"
GET mykey
example.explanation: The first command creates the key and returns 1; the second does nothing and returns 0, so GET still returns Hello.

useCases.title: Conditional initialization
useCases.scenario: Prevent a one-time initialization value from being overwritten when multiple clients race to create the same key.

useCases.title: Simple locking primitive
useCases.scenario: Claim a key as a basic coordination marker so only the client receiving 1 proceeds.

useCases.title: Duplicate detection
useCases.scenario: Use the return code to distinguish the first insertion from later duplicate attempts.

interview.question: What does SETNX do?
interview.answer: SETNX stores the supplied string only if the key does not exist. It returns 1 when it creates the key and 0 when the key already exists.
interview.followUp: How should new code express the same condition? Use SET with the NX option, which is the documented replacement for SETNX.

interview.question: What are SETNX's arguments and behavior when the key already exists?
interview.answer: The command takes exactly a key and a value: SETNX key value. The value is written only when the key is absent; an existing key is left unchanged.
interview.followUp: What happens if the existing key contains a different data type? SETNX performs a presence check and does not replace the existing value.

interview.question: How has SETNX historically been used for locking?
interview.answer: A successful result of 1 indicates that the client acquired the lock key; a result of 0 means another client already holds it. The documented pattern releases the lock with DEL.
interview.followUp: What limitation should be considered for a production lock? A robust design needs an expiration and ownership-safe release strategy rather than relying only on a bare SETNX key.

keyPoints: It conditionally creates a key with a string value.
An existing key remains unchanged, including its current value.
The name describes its set-if-absent semantics.
The integer result is 0 when the conditional write does not happen.
The integer result is 1 when the command creates the key.
The historical locking pattern stores a future validity timestamp as the lock value.
gotchas: SETNX is deprecated; for new code, prefer SET with the NX option.
A lock implemented with SETNX requires an explicit DEL release step, so the lock key must be managed carefully.

SETRANGE.summary: Overwrites part of a Redis string from a specified zero-based offset. It pads with zero bytes when necessary and returns the string's resulting length.
SETRANGE.explanation: SETRANGE replaces bytes in the string stored at a key, beginning at a zero-based offset and continuing for the length of the supplied value. If the key is missing, Redis treats it as an empty string; if the offset extends past the current value, Redis inserts zero-byte padding before writing. The command returns the resulting string length.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: The zero-based offset at which to start overwriting. The string is zero-padded if the offset is beyond the current length.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The string to write at the offset.

SETRANGE.returns: Integer reply: the length of the string after it was modified by the command.

example.title: Overwrite part of a string
example.code:
SET key1 "Hello World"
SETRANGE key1 6 "Redis"
GET key1
example.explanation: Writes "Redis" starting at byte offset 6, then reads the resulting string: "Hello Redis".

useCases.title: Random-access string storage
useCases.scenario: Treat a Redis string as a byte-addressable sequence and update a region without replacing the entire value.

useCases.title: Dense byte arrays
useCases.scenario: Store compact per-entity byte values in a large string, using offsets as positions.

useCases.title: Range-based string updates
useCases.scenario: Combine with GETRANGE to read and update fixed regions of a string.

interview.question: What does SETRANGE do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: SETRANGE uses a zero-based offset and overwrites the existing string for the entire length of the new value. If the write extends beyond the current end, Redis pads the gap with zero bytes and returns the final string length.
interview.followUp: What happens when the key does not exist? Redis treats it as an empty string, creates the string, and places the supplied value at the requested offset.

interview.question: Explain SETRANGE's arguments.
interview.answer: The command's syntax is `SETRANGE key offset value`. `key` identifies the string, `offset` is the zero-based starting position, and `value` is the string written there.
interview.followUp: How should an offset beyond the existing value be interpreted? It causes zero-byte padding before the new value is stored.

interview.question: What is SETRANGE's time complexity?
interview.answer: The documented complexity is O(1), excluding the time needed to copy the new string in place. When the value being copied is longer, the complexity is O(M), where M is its length.
interview.followUp: What storage pattern does Redis documentation associate with SETRANGE and GETRANGE? They can treat strings as linear arrays with O(1) random access.

keyPoints: It modifies an existing Redis string in place, beginning at the supplied position.
The overwrite spans every byte in the replacement value.
Offsets count from zero, so the first byte is position 0.
The result is the string's length after the write, not the number of bytes changed.
Together with GETRANGE, it supports array-like random access over string data.
For a non-small replacement, runtime grows with the replacement value's length.
gotchas: The offset cannot exceed 536870911 because Redis strings are limited to 512 MB.
Writing beyond the current end enlarges the string and inserts zero bytes between the old content and the new value.
A missing key is created as a string large enough to contain the value at the requested offset.

SMEMBERS.summary: Returns every member of the set stored at a key. The result contains the set's complete, unordered membership.
SMEMBERS.explanation: SMEMBERS reads the complete set stored at the specified key and returns its members as an unordered collection. It is equivalent to running SINTER with that one key, and its work grows linearly with the set size.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key containing the set whose members should be returned.

SMEMBERS.returns: All members of the set at the key; RESP2 represents them as an array reply, while RESP3 represents them as a set reply.

example.title: Read all set members
example.code:
SADD myset "Hello" "World"
SMEMBERS myset
