example.explanation: Adds two values to a Redis set, then retrieves every member.

useCases.title: Read set membership
useCases.scenario: Inspect the current contents of a set during application logic or debugging.

useCases.title: Materialize a set
useCases.scenario: Load all participants, tags, or identifiers represented by a set when the collection is suitably small.

useCases.title: Support set-based workflows
useCases.scenario: Compare a set's full contents with another collection after retrieving its members.

interview.question: What does SMEMBERS return, and what is its complexity?
interview.answer: SMEMBERS returns all members held by the set at a key. Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the set cardinality.
interview.followUp: How would you read a very large set incrementally? Use SSCAN, which iterates through set members in batches instead of retrieving the entire collection at once.

interview.question: What argument does SMEMBERS require, and what does the reply look like?
interview.answer: The command takes one required argument: the key containing the set. The result is an array in RESP2 and a set in RESP3.
interview.followUp: Does SMEMBERS sort its output? No; set membership has no ordering guarantee, so consumers should not depend on result order.

interview.question: When was SMEMBERS introduced and what kind of operation is it?
interview.answer: SMEMBERS is a read-only set command that returns every member stored at the supplied key. It has been available since Redis Open Source 1.0.0.
interview.followUp: What happens if the key contains a non-set value? Redis reports a wrong-type error rather than treating the value as a set.

keyPoints: Use SMEMBERS to retrieve the complete membership of a Redis set.
Its sole argument is the key whose value is the target set.
The command has existed since Redis Open Source 1.0.0.
Redis classifies SMEMBERS as a read operation for set data and marks it as slow.
gotchas: SMEMBERS does not impose ordering; treat the result as a set rather than relying on element positions.
Retrieving a large set can be expensive because the command processes every member.

STRLEN.summary: Returns the length of the string value stored at a key. Missing keys return 0, while keys holding non-string values cause an error.
STRLEN.explanation: STRLEN reads the string stored at a key and returns its length as an integer. If the key is absent, it returns 0; if the key contains another Redis data type, the command returns an error.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key containing the string to measure.

STRLEN.returns: Integer reply: the length of the string stored at key, or 0 when the key does not exist.

example.title: Measure a Redis string
example.code:
redis-cli SET mykey "Hello world"
redis-cli STRLEN mykey
# (integer) 11
redis-cli STRLEN missing-key
# (integer) 0
example.explanation: Stores a string, measures its length, then demonstrates the zero result for an absent key.

useCases.title: Check string size
useCases.scenario: Validate or inspect stored text before processing it.

useCases.title: Inspect key contents
useCases.scenario: Distinguish an empty string from a missing key when combined with existence checks.

useCases.title: Operational diagnostics
useCases.scenario: Measure a Redis string in scripts, monitoring commands, or command-line workflows.

interview.question: What does STRLEN return for an existing string and for a missing key?
interview.answer: STRLEN takes one key and returns an integer reply containing the length of the string stored there. A missing key produces 0.
interview.followUp: What happens if the key stores a list? Redis returns an error because STRLEN only accepts string values.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of STRLEN?
interview.answer: Its documented complexity is O(1), so retrieving the length does not require scanning the string contents.
interview.followUp: How would you measure a JSON string instead? Use JSON.STRLEN with a key and optional path.

interview.question: What is the command signature and required argument?
interview.answer: The command syntax is `STRLEN key`. The required argument is the name of the key whose string value should be measured.
interview.followUp: What related command appends data while working with a string key? APPEND adds a value and creates the key if it does not exist.

keyPoints: STRLEN reports the character/byte length of the string value associated with the supplied key.
The result is an integer, and an absent key is represented by zero rather than an error.
Its only required argument is the key name.
For the documented `Hello world` example, STRLEN returns 11.
gotchas: The key must contain a Redis string; using STRLEN on another data type produces an error.

SUBSCRIBE.summary: Subscribes the client to one or more exact channel names. Redis then pushes matching published messages and subscription confirmations through that connection.
SUBSCRIBE.explanation: SUBSCRIBE registers the current client for one or more exact channel names. After the client enters subscribed mode, Redis pushes matching published messages over the connection and sends a subscription confirmation for each channel; with RESP2, only a limited set of commands remains available until the client leaves that mode.

parameters.name: channel [channel ...]
parameters.description: One or more exact channel names to which the client should subscribe.

SUBSCRIBE.returns: On success, Redis does not return a conventional value. Instead, it pushes one subscription confirmation message for each requested channel, with `subscribe` as the first element.

example.title: Subscribe to an exact channel
example.code: SUBSCRIBE cache:events
example.explanation: Run this command in redis-cli to enter Pub/Sub mode and listen for messages published to the exact channel `cache:events`. The client remains waiting for pushed messages until it unsubscribes or exits.

useCases.title: Exact-topic event delivery
useCases.scenario: A service needs real-time notifications for a known topic such as `orders:created`.

useCases.title: Multiple channel subscriptions
useCases.scenario: Several known application topics should share one subscriber connection.

useCases.title: Interactive Pub/Sub monitoring
useCases.scenario: A lightweight client needs to observe live channel traffic during development or operations.

interview.question: What does SUBSCRIBE do?
interview.answer: SUBSCRIBE takes one or more channel names and switches the connection into subscribed mode. Redis pushes a confirmation for each subscription, followed by messages published to those channels.
interview.followUp: How would you subscribe to a family of channels? Use PSUBSCRIBE with a pattern, because SUBSCRIBE matches only the explicitly named channels.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of SUBSCRIBE?
interview.answer: The command's complexity is O(N), where N is the number of channels being subscribed to. Each specified channel contributes to the subscription operation.
interview.followUp: What is the practical implication of subscribing to many channels? The command processes each channel, so the work grows linearly with the number supplied.

interview.question: Which commands are allowed after entering subscribed state?
interview.answer: A RESP2 client in subscribed state is restricted to subscription-management commands and a few connection commands such as PING and QUIT. A RESP3 client can issue any commands while remaining subscribed.
interview.followUp: How can a RESP2 client return to normal command use? It must unsubscribe from its channels and leave subscribed mode.

keyPoints: The command creates exact-match subscriptions for every channel named in the request.
At least one channel is required, and multiple channels can be supplied in the same command.
Redis sends one subscription-confirmation push message per channel after successful registration.
Published messages are delivered to every client subscribed to the corresponding channel.
The operation scales linearly with the number of channels in the request.
The command has been available since Redis Open Source 2.0.0.
gotchas: In RESP2 subscribed mode, do not send ordinary commands; use the permitted subscription, unsubscription, PING, RESET, or QUIT commands. RESP3 permits any commands while subscribed.
SUBSCRIBE provides exact channel matching, not pattern matching; use PSUBSCRIBE when a glob-style channel pattern is required.

TOUCH.summary: TOUCH updates the last-access time of each supplied key that exists and returns how many supplied keys were found. It does not alter key values.
TOUCH.explanation: TOUCH updates the last-access time for each named key that exists, without changing its value. It returns how many supplied keys were found and touched; the operation costs O(N), where N is the number of keys listed.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: One or more key names whose access times should be updated when the keys exist.

TOUCH.returns: Integer reply: the number of supplied keys that exist after their last-access times are updated.

example.title: Touch an active session key
example.code:
SET session:42 active
TOUCH session:42 missing:key
example.explanation: Refreshes the access time for the existing session key; the command returns 1 because only one of the two keys exists.

useCases.title: Cache access tracking
useCases.scenario: Refresh recency for cached entries while leaving their values unchanged.

useCases.title: Batch existence measurement
useCases.scenario: Touch several potentially present keys and use the count to measure partial existence.

useCases.title: Eviction-aware workflows
useCases.scenario: Keep selected keys active for LRU/LFU-oriented access accounting.

interview.question: What does Redis TOUCH do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: TOUCH refreshes the last-access time of every supplied key that exists and returns the count of those existing keys. It does not modify the stored values.
interview.followUp: What is its complexity? O(N), where N is the number of keys supplied for touching.

interview.question: What is the syntax and result semantics of TOUCH?
interview.answer: The command accepts one or more key names using the syntax TOUCH key [key ...]. The integer result is the number of supplied keys that exist.
interview.followUp: How would a caller detect partial success? Compare the returned count with the number of keys sent.

interview.question: What is the complexity of TOUCH?
interview.answer: TOUCH has linear complexity in the number of keys it processes: O(N). This matters when a request contains many key names.
interview.followUp: What design response follows from that complexity? Keep batches appropriately sized when access-time refreshes are performed at scale.

keyPoints: For each existing key, Redis refreshes its last-access timestamp.
The command requires at least one key and supports a variable-length key list.
The integer reply reports how many supplied names currently exist.
Processing cost grows linearly with the number of keys in the request.
gotchas: The result counts existing keys only, so nonexistent names contribute zero.
Large key lists increase work linearly; avoid treating TOUCH as a constant-time operation.

TTL.summary: Returns a key's remaining expiration time in seconds. It distinguishes missing keys from existing keys that have no expiration.
TTL.explanation: TTL inspects a key's expiration and returns the number of seconds until Redis removes it. It returns special negative values when the key is missing or exists without an expiration, allowing clients to distinguish those states.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key whose remaining expiration time should be inspected.

TTL.returns: An integer number of seconds remaining; -1 if the key exists without an expiration; -2 if the key does not exist.

example.title: Check a key's remaining lifetime
example.code:
SET session:123 active EX 60
TTL session:123
example.explanation: Stores a key with a 60-second expiration, then reports its remaining lifetime in seconds.

useCases.title: Cache lifetime monitoring
useCases.scenario: Inspect how long a cached value can remain before Redis removes it.

useCases.title: Session and token expiry checks
useCases.scenario: Check whether a session or token key is nearing expiration.

useCases.title: Key-state diagnostics
useCases.scenario: Identify whether a key is absent, persistent, or configured to expire.

interview.question: What does TTL do?
interview.answer: TTL returns the remaining time to live for a key in seconds. It is an introspection command, so it checks expiration without changing the key.
interview.followUp: How would you obtain finer resolution? Use PTTL, which reports the corresponding expiration information in milliseconds.

interview.question: What do TTL's negative return values mean?
interview.answer: TTL returns -2 when the key does not exist and -1 when the key exists but has no expiration. A nonnegative result is the remaining lifetime in seconds.
interview.followUp: How can a key acquire an expiration? Set one with EXPIRE, or write it using an expiration option such as SET with EX.

interview.question: When should TTL be preferred over PTTL?
interview.answer: Use TTL when second-level precision is sufficient for checking cache or session lifetime. For millisecond resolution, use PTTL instead.
interview.followUp: What should a client do when TTL returns -2? Treat the value as absent and avoid assuming that an expiration is merely near.

keyPoints: TTL reports the remaining lifetime only for a key with a configured timeout.
The command lets clients inspect the lifetime in seconds without retrieving the stored value.
The result estimates how long the key remains part of Redis's dataset.
Use PTTL when the application needs the same check at millisecond resolution.
gotchas: A missing key produces -2, not a normal zero-second lifetime.
A persistent key produces -1, so do not interpret it as imminent expiration.

TYPE.summary: TYPE reports the Redis data type stored at a key. It returns none when the key does not exist.
TYPE.explanation: TYPE examines the value associated with one key and returns its Redis data-type name. If the key is absent, it returns none; otherwise the documented result can identify strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, streams, or vector sets.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key whose value type should be returned.

TYPE.returns: Simple string reply: the type of key, or none when key does not exist.

example.title: Inspect Redis value types
example.code:
redis-cli <<'EOF'
SET profile:name Ada
HSET profile:stats visits 3
TYPE profile:name
TYPE profile:stats
TYPE profile:missing
EOF
example.explanation: Creates a string and a hash, then reports each stored value's Redis type or none for the absent key.

useCases.title: Validate a data structure
useCases.scenario: Inspect a key before issuing type-specific commands.

useCases.title: Debug key contents
useCases.scenario: Diagnose unexpected values in a shared keyspace.

useCases.title: Check cache state
useCases.scenario: Distinguish missing cache entries from populated entries.

interview.question: What does TYPE return for a missing key?
interview.answer: TYPE takes one key and returns a simple string naming the stored value's type. If the key does not exist, the result is none.
interview.followUp: How would you distinguish an absent key from a key holding a string? Check whether TYPE returns none; string indicates an existing string value.

interview.question: What is the syntax and required argument?
interview.answer: The command syntax is TYPE key. The required key argument is the name of the key whose value should be inspected.
interview.followUp: What should be done when the key name is dynamic? Pass the key as a properly encoded command argument and interpret the returned type string.

interview.question: Which Redis types can TYPE report?
interview.answer: TYPE can report string, list, set, zset, hash, stream, or vectorset. It is useful before selecting commands that operate on a particular Redis data structure.
interview.followUp: Why must command selection still be validated after inspection? The key's type can change between separate commands, so atomic or error-handling strategies may be needed.

keyPoints: TYPE converts the stored value's data structure into a type-name string.
Recognized results include string, list, set, and sorted set values.
The command also recognizes hashes, streams, and vector sets.
Its required input is the key name to inspect.
The response is a simple string containing the type, or none when the key is missing.
gotchas: An absent key produces none rather than an error, so callers should handle that result separately from a stored type.

UNLINK.summary: UNLINK asynchronously deletes one or more Redis keys. It removes keys from the keyspace promptly while reclaiming their memory in a background thread.
UNLINK.explanation: UNLINK removes the specified keys from Redis's keyspace immediately, while memory reclamation runs asynchronously in another thread. It accepts one or more keys, ignores keys that do not exist, and returns how many keys were unlinked.

parameters.name: key [key ...]
parameters.description: One or more keys to delete asynchronously.

UNLINK.returns: Integer reply: the number of keys that were unlinked.

example.title: Asynchronously remove keys
example.code:
SET key1 "Hello"
SET key2 "World"
UNLINK key1 key2 key3
example.explanation: Creates two keys, then asynchronously unlinks them; the missing third key is ignored.

useCases.title: Delete large cache entries
useCases.scenario: Removing large cached values without synchronously blocking Redis's main thread.

useCases.title: Best-effort multi-key cleanup
useCases.scenario: Deleting several known keys while tolerating keys that may already be absent.

useCases.title: Cluster-aware cleanup
useCases.scenario: Performing non-blocking key removal in a clustered deployment after checking multi-key constraints.

interview.question: Why use UNLINK instead of DEL for large values?
interview.answer: UNLINK removes one or more keys without making memory reclamation block the main Redis thread. It unlinks each key from the keyspace and performs the heavier reclamation work asynchronously.
interview.followUp: How does its complexity compare with DEL? UNLINK is O(1) per removed key regardless of value size in the command path, followed by O(N) reclamation work in another thread.

interview.question: What does UNLINK return?
interview.answer: The command accepts one or more keys using the form UNLINK key [key ...]. Missing keys are ignored, and the integer reply reports how many keys were actually unlinked.
interview.followUp: What does a reply of 2 mean for three supplied keys? Exactly two supplied keys existed and were unlinked; the third was absent or otherwise not counted.

interview.question: What cluster consideration applies to multi-key UNLINK?
interview.answer: UNLINK can remove multiple keys in one command, but clustered Redis environments impose multi-key behavior constraints. Keys may need to satisfy the cluster's requirements for multi-key operations.
interview.followUp: What should be checked before issuing a multi-key UNLINK in a cluster? Review Redis's multi-key operation rules and ensure the selected keys are valid for the target cluster topology.

keyPoints: The unlinking operation is O(1) per key, independent of the size of the value stored there.
Memory reclamation is proportional to the deleted object's allocations and is handled by another thread.
Supplying a nonexistent key does not produce an error or increase the returned count.
The keyspace no longer exposes the unlinked keys after the command processes them.
The required argument is a variadic list containing at least one key.
gotchas: In clustered Redis, multi-key behavior has cluster-specific constraints; consult the multi-key operations rules when the keys may be distributed across shards.
A successful reply means the keys were unlinked from the keyspace, not that all associated memory has already been reclaimed.

ZADD.summary: Adds members with scores to a sorted set, updating existing members and creating the key when needed. Options can restrict updates, count changed entries, or increment one member's score.
ZADD.explanation: ZADD adds score-member pairs to the sorted set at key. A missing key is created; an existing member is repositioned when its score changes. Options can restrict updates, count changed entries, or return the new score while incrementing one member.
ZADD.syntax: ZADD key [NX | XX] [GT | LT] [CH] [INCR] score member [score member ...]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Name of the key that holds the sorted set.

parameters.name: score member [score member ...]
parameters.description: One or more score-member pairs; each score is a double-precision floating-point number.

parameters.name: NX
parameters.description: Add only new members.

parameters.name: XX
parameters.description: Update only existing members.

parameters.name: CH
parameters.description: Count changed members, including score updates.

parameters.name: INCR
parameters.description: Increment one member's score instead of setting it.

parameters.name: GT
parameters.description: Update only when the new score is greater.

parameters.name: LT
parameters.description: Update only when the new score is less.

ZADD.returns: Integer reply: newly added members by default, or newly added and updated members with CH. With INCR, returns the updated score as a double. A null reply is returned when a conditional NX, XX, GT, or LT operation is aborted.

example.title: Add and conditionally update leaderboard scores
example.code:
redis-cli ZADD leaderboard 100 alice 125 bob
redis-cli ZADD leaderboard GT 130 alice
redis-cli ZRANGE leaderboard 0 -1 REV WITHSCORES
example.explanation: Adds two members, raises Alice's score only when the new score is greater, then lists the leaderboard from highest to lowest score.

useCases.title: Leaderboards
useCases.scenario: Maintain a ranking that changes as players or entities receive scores.

useCases.title: Priority ordering
useCases.scenario: Store items ordered by numeric priority for range and rank queries.

useCases.title: Score increments
useCases.scenario: Atomically update a single member's score while retrieving its new value.

interview.question: What does ZADD do?
interview.answer: ZADD inserts members into a sorted set and associates each with a double-precision score. If a member already exists, its score is updated and the member is placed according to the resulting order; a nonexistent key is created.
interview.followUp: How does ZADD behave when the key has another type? It returns an error because the key must hold a sorted set.

interview.question: How do CH and INCR affect the reply?
interview.answer: Without CH, the integer reply counts only newly added members. With CH, it counts both newly added and updated members.
interview.followUp: What does INCR return? It returns the member's updated score as a double, or a null reply when the conditional operation is not performed.

interview.question: What are the conditional ZADD options?
interview.answer: NX permits only new members, while XX permits updates only for existing members. GT and LT constrain updates to cases where the new score is respectively greater or less than the current score.
interview.followUp: Can GT and LT be used together? No; the mutually exclusive option pairs must not be combined, and INCR permits only one score-member pair.

keyPoints: ZADD supports one or many score-member pairs in a single command.
A missing key becomes a new sorted set containing the supplied members.
Changing an existing member's score also restores its sorted-set position.
Scores use double-precision floating-point representations, including the documented infinity values.
The default integer result reports how many members were newly inserted.
CH changes counting to include score updates as well as insertions.
gotchas: The target key must contain a sorted set; ZADD fails with a wrong-type error for other Redis data types.
INCR mode accepts exactly one score-member pair, unlike ordinary ZADD calls that can update multiple pairs.
When a conditional option prevents the operation, the reply is null rather than an integer count.

ZRANGE.summary: Returns members from a sorted set selected by rank, score, or lexicographical range. Optional reverse ordering, pagination, and score output support ranking, filtering, and windowed reads.
ZRANGE.explanation: ZRANGE reads members from a sorted set using an index range by default. BYSCORE changes the bounds to scores, BYLEX changes them to lexicographical member values, REV reverses the result order, LIMIT paginates matches, and WITHSCORES includes each member's score.
ZRANGE.syntax: ZRANGE key start stop [BYSCORE | BYLEX] [REV] [LIMIT offset count] [WITHSCORES]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Name of the sorted-set key.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: Starting rank, score bound, or lexicographical bound, depending on the selected mode.

parameters.name: stop
parameters.description: Ending rank, score bound, or lexicographical bound, depending on the selected mode.

parameters.name: BYSCORE | BYLEX
parameters.description: Select score-based or lexicographical bounds.

parameters.name: REV
parameters.description: Reverse the result order and interpretation of the range.

parameters.name: LIMIT offset count
parameters.description: Skip offset matches and return up to count matches.

parameters.name: WITHSCORES
parameters.description: Include scores alongside members.

ZRANGE.returns: An array of matching sorted-set members; with WITHSCORES, each member is accompanied by its score. A non-overlapping range returns an empty array.

example.title: Rank and score range queries
example.code:
ZADD leaderboard 120 alice 95 bob 110 carol
ZRANGE leaderboard 0 -1 WITHSCORES
ZRANGE leaderboard 100 120 BYSCORE REV LIMIT 0 2
example.explanation: Adds three members, lists them by rank with scores, then retrieves up to two members whose scores fall in the selected range in descending score order.

useCases.title: Leaderboards and ranking pages
useCases.scenario: Fetch a page of leaderboard entries by rank, optionally including their scores.

useCases.title: Score-range filtering
useCases.scenario: Select records whose sorted-set scores fall between two bounds.

useCases.title: Lexicographical indexing
useCases.scenario: Use equal-score members and BYLEX bounds to retrieve a name or identifier interval.

interview.question: How does default ZRANGE indexing work?
interview.answer: By default, ZRANGE interprets start and stop as zero-based rank indexes, and both bounds are inclusive. Negative indexes count backward from the end, with -1 representing the final member.
interview.followUp: How can it retrieve the highest-scoring members? Use REV together with BYSCORE, then apply LIMIT, for example: ZRANGE key +inf -inf BYSCORE REV LIMIT 0 10.

interview.question: How does a score-based query differ from the default query?
interview.answer: BYSCORE makes the two bounds score limits instead of indexes. Score bounds can be inclusive or exclusive, and special values such as -inf and +inf can represent unbounded ends.
interview.followUp: How would you return scores as well? Add WITHSCORES; the response alternates each returned member with its score.

interview.question: What options control ordering, pagination, and returned data?
interview.answer: ZRANGE supports BYLEX for member-name ranges, REV for reverse ordering, LIMIT offset count for pagination, and WITHSCORES for returning scores. Its complexity is O(log(N)+M), where M is the number of returned elements.
interview.followUp: Why should a caller avoid unrestricted large reads? Because M grows with the result size, so limiting the requested range reduces work and response size.

keyPoints: The command reads members from the sorted set stored at the specified key.
One command supports rank-based, score-based, and lexicographical range selection.
Negative rank indexes address members relative to the set's end.
An oversized ending rank is clamped to the last available member.
gotchas: The start and stop bounds are inclusive. Use a parenthesis on score or lexicographical bounds when an exclusive boundary is required.
Invalid or non-overlapping index ranges return an empty list rather than an error.
